name: Electrolyte skincare

card.summary: Skincare marketed with minerals such as sodium, magnesium and potassium to support skin hydration and a plump, healthy look.
card.note: A marketing category rather than a defined product class.

quick.overview:
Electrolyte skincare covers creams, masks, mists and serums marketed with minerals such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium and chloride. The idea borrows from electrolyte drinks: because these minerals attract water, brands say they help skin hold on to moisture.

The appearance goal is skin that looks hydrated, plump and smooth. Dermatologists quoted in beauty media say the concept makes sense in theory but that high-quality studies of these products are lacking.
quick.how: Products are used like other moisturizers or overnight masks, after cleansing, often with humectants such as glycerin or hyaluronic acid, ceramides and sunscreen. Dermatologists quoted by Healthline mention people with dry, sensitive or eczema-prone skin and people who sweat a lot as possible users.
quick.risks: Risk is generally low. Propylene glycol can irritate or cause allergy in some people, and heavy occlusive creams can contribute to acne in people prone to it, according to Healthline. Fragrance and other ingredients can also irritate sensitive skin.

lead: Electrolyte skincare is a marketing label for topical products built around minerals the body uses as electrolytes, including potassium, sodium, calcium, chloride, phosphate and magnesium.[1] It is used to make skin look and feel more hydrated, plump and smooth, and appears in moisturizers, overnight masks, thermal-water sprays and gel creams.[1][2]

Brands say the minerals' electrical charge draws water into skin, helps it retain moisture and supports the skin barrier against environmental stress.[2] Several dermatologists have commented on the trend: one told Healthline the idea makes sense "on paper" but that she had not seen high-quality studies, while another noted that water and electrolytes applied to skin evaporate quickly.[1] Another, Dr. Lisa Kellett, said there is little evidence-based medicine supporting their use in skincare.[2]
The category overlaps with the wider interest in mineral-rich skincare covered by British Vogue in 2022, which included magnesium, zinc, copper, algae and colloidal metals.[3]

chain: Minerals are said to attract and hold water in the skin
Skin looks more hydrated, plump and smooth
angle.text: Brands position electrolyte products as hydration support for the skin surface. Users apply them as moisturizers, masks or mists to get a smoother, more hydrated look, often alongside ceramides, glycerin or hyaluronic acid.

paras: The term has no formal definition, and formulations vary. Healthline lists the electrolytes involved as potassium, sodium, calcium, chloride, phosphate and magnesium.[1] Cosmetics magazine describes ingredients such as potassium, sodium bicarbonate and chloride, and notes one brand that uses electrolyte-rich aquifer water in place of demineralized water.[2]

Products named in coverage include Paula's Choice Water-Infusing Electrolyte Moisturizer, Drunk Elephant F-Balm Electrolyte Waterfacial Mask (listed at $72), Omy Lab Aquifer Hydra-Thermal Water and Neutrogena Hydro Boost Gel Cream with hyaluronic acid and electrolytes.[1][2]

The central argument is that electrolytes attract water, so they may help skin retain moisture.[1] Brands add that the charge of the minerals pulls water in and strengthens the barrier.[2] Dermatologist Bruce Robinson told Healthline that formulas pairing electrolytes with skin-identical molecules such as lactate, gluconate or pyroglutamic acid (PCA), plus ceramides, glycerin or hyaluronic acid, may help the minerals work better.[1]
Dermatologist Ife Rodney pointed out that water and electrolytes applied to skin evaporate quickly, so it is unclear whether they are absorbed well enough to raise hydration.[1]

Healthline's dermatologists say the products may suit people who work out a lot or have dry, irritated or sensitive skin or certain types of eczema, and that they are not necessarily better than often cheaper conventional moisturizers.[1] A broad-spectrum sunscreen is advised in the morning if the moisturizer lacks SPF.[1]

Healthline notes that propylene glycol can cause allergy or irritation in some people and that occlusive creams may cause acne, so noncomedogenic formulas are suggested for those prone to breakouts.[1] Other cosmetic ingredients such as fragrance can irritate sensitive skin.
No studies found. Dermatologists quoted in the press describe a lack of high-quality studies on electrolyte-labelled creams.[1][2]

timeline.event: British Vogue covers minerals in skincare, listing magnesium-containing hydrators such as Paula's Choice Water-Infusing Electrolyte Moisturizer.[3]
Cosmetics magazine publishes a feature on electrolyte skincare, with dermatologist and brand perspectives.[2]
